claim: The Rho GTPase Rac1 activates the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC) to drive Arp2/3 complex-mediated actin polymerization.
source: The Rho GTPase Rac1 activates the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC) to drive Arp2/3 complex-mediated actin polymerization, which underpins diverse cellular processes.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by the entire body of work and established scientific knowledge.

claim: The structure of a WRC-Rac1 complex was determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here we report the structure of a WRC-Rac1 complex determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cryo-EM methodology and presents structural data.

claim: Rac1 is not located at the binding site on the Sra1 subunit of the WRC previously identified by mutagenesis and biochemical data.
source: Surprisingly, Rac1 is not located at the binding site on the Sra1 subunit of the WRC previously identified by mutagenesis and biochemical data.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure showing Rac1 at a different location than predicted.

claim: Rac1 binds to a distinct, conserved site on the opposite end of Sra1.
source: Rather, it binds to a distinct, conserved site on the opposite end of Sra1.
evidence: The cryo-EM structure reveals Rac1 binding at a new site.

claim: Rac1 binds to both the previously identified site (A Site) and the newly identified site (D Site) on the WRC.
source: Biophysical and biochemical data on WRC mutants confirm that Rac1 binds to both sites, with the newly identified site having higher affinity and both sites required for WRC activation.
evidence: Multiple biochemical assays including pull-downs, AUC, and membrane recruitment assays support this claim.

claim: The newly identified D Site has higher affinity for Rac1 than the previously identified A Site.
source: Biophysical and biochemical data on WRC mutants confirm that Rac1 binds to both sites, with the newly identified site having higher affinity and both sites required for WRC activation.
evidence: Equilibrium pull-down assays show approximately 40-fold difference in affinity.

claim: Both Rac1 binding sites are required for WRC activation.
source: Biophysical and biochemical data on WRC mutants confirm that Rac1 binds to both sites, with the newly identified site having higher affinity and both sites required for WRC activation.
evidence: Actin assembly assays show that mutations at either site abolish activation.

claim: The WRC is activated by simultaneous engagement of two Rac1 molecules.
source: Our data reveal that the WRC is activated by simultaneous engagement of two Rac1 molecules, suggesting a mechanism by which cells may sense the density of active Rac1 at membranes to precisely control actin assembly.
evidence: AUC data show 2:1 stoichiometry and actin assembly data show requirement for both sites.

claim: Dynamic rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton play central roles in cellular processes ranging from cell migration and adhesion to endocytosis and intracellular vesicle trafficking.
source: Dynamic rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton play central roles in cellular processes, ranging from cell migration and adhesion to endocytosis and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Skau and Waterman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: WASP family proteins integrate diverse upstream signals and transmit them through their conserved VCA sequence to the Arp2/3 complex.
source: These proteins integrate a diverse array of upstream signals and transmit them through their conserved VCA sequence to the Arp2/3 complex, which, in turn, nucleates actin filaments to create branched actin networks at membranes (Campellone and Welch, 2010; Padrick and Rosen, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex nucleates actin filaments to create branched actin networks at membranes.
source: These proteins integrate a diverse array of upstream signals and transmit them through their conserved VCA sequence to the Arp2/3 complex, which, in turn, nucleates actin filaments to create branched actin networks at membranes (Campellone and Welch, 2010; Padrick and Rosen, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In most WASP family proteins, the VCA element is inhibited in the resting state.
source: In most WASP family proteins, the VCA element is inhibited in the resting state.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations and established knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of the VCA element is mediated either by autoinhibition within a single polypeptide chain (as in WASP and N-WASP) or by trans-inhibition within large multi-protein assemblies (as in WAVE and WASH).
source: Inhibition is mediated either by autoinhibition within a single polypeptide chain, as in WASP and N-WASP, or by trans-inhibition within large multi-protein assemblies, as in WAVE and WASH (Rotty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Multiple signals including binding to ligands and covalent modifications often act cooperatively to relieve inhibition and recruit WASP proteins to their sites of action at membranes.
source: Multiple signals, including binding to ligands (e.g. Rho family GTPases, phosphoinositide lipids and membrane receptors) and covalent modifications (e.g. phosphorylation and ubiquitination), often act cooperatively to relieve inhibition and concomitantly recruit WASP proteins to their sites of action at membranes (Chen et al., 2014a, 2010; Hao et al., 2013; Lebensohn and Kirschner, 2009; Padrick and Rosen, 2010; Prehoda et al., 2000; Torres and Rosen, 2003; 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: WAVE1, WAVE2 and WAVE3 are essential to actin dynamics needed for normal development and function of most eukaryotic organisms.
source: The WASP family members WAVE1, WAVE2 and WAVE3 are essential to actin dynamics needed for normal development and function of most eukaryotic organisms, and are also implicated in many cancers (Bisi et al., 2013; Lane et al., 2014; Takenawa and Suetsugu, 2007; Yanagisawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: WAVE proteins are implicated in many cancers.
source: The WASP family members WAVE1, WAVE2 and WAVE3 are essential to actin dynamics needed for normal development and function of most eukaryotic organisms, and are also implicated in many cancers (Bisi et al., 2013; Lane et al., 2014; Takenawa and Suetsugu, 2007; Yanagisawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Each WAVE protein functions exclusively within a 400 kDa heteropentameric assembly termed the WAVE Regulatory Complex (WRC).
source: In cells, each WAVE protein functions exclusively within a 400 kDa, heteropentameric assembly, termed the WAVE Regulatory Complex (WRC), which also contains the proteins Sra1, Nap1, Abi2, and HSPC300 (or their homologs) (Stovold et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The WRC contains the proteins Sra1, Nap1, Abi2, HSPC300, and WAVE.
source: In cells, each WAVE protein functions exclusively within a 400 kDa, heteropentameric assembly, termed the WAVE Regulatory Complex (WRC), which also contains the proteins Sra1, Nap1, Abi2, and HSPC300 (or their homologs) (Stovold et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Sra1 and Nap1 form an elongated dimer of about 100 × 100 × 200 Å.
source: The structure revealed that Sra1 and Nap1 form an elongated dimer of about 100 × 100 ×200 Å.
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: WAVE1, Abi2 and HSPC300 form a trimer as an elongated 4-helix bundle.
source: WAVE1, Abi2 and HSPC300 form a trimer as an elongated 4-helix bundle, which aligns along the long axis of the Sra1/Nap1 dimer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An extended sequence of ~90 amino acids from WAVE1 'meanders' across the surface of Sra1 as a loose collection of loops and helices.
source: Immediately following the helix bundle, an extended sequence of ~90 a.a. from WAVE1 'meanders' across the surface of Sra1 as a loose collection of loops and helices (the meander region).
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: The VCA element of WAVE1 is sequestered at the VCA-binding site by multiple interactions between its V and C helices and a group of helices from both Sra1 and the meander region of WAVE1 itself.
source: The VCA element of WAVE1 is sequestered at the VCA-binding site by multiple interactions between its V and C helices and a group of helices from both Sra1 and the meander region of WAVE1 itself, explaining how WAVE1 is inhibited within the WRC (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: The tethered Rac1 protected the WRC from binding to GST-Rac1 much more efficiently than the un-tethered Rac1 protected the wild type WRC.
source: Based on experiments measuring binding to immobilized GST-Rac1, the tethered Rac1 protected the WRC from binding to GST-Rac1 much more efficiently than the un-tethered Rac1 protected the wild type WRC, suggesting the tethered Rac1 binds the WRC in a physiologically relevant manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by competition pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Q61L mutation abolishes the GTP hydrolysis activity of Rac1, maintaining the protein in the GTP-bound state.
source: The Q61L mutation abolishes the GTP hydrolysis activity of Rac1 (Der et al., 1986), maintaining the protein in the GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The P29S mutation was identified as one of the major somatic mutations in melanoma.
source: The P29S mutation was identified as one of the major somatic mutations in melanoma (Hodis et al., 2012; Krauthammer et al., 2012), and was shown to increase the affinity of Rac1 for the effectors PAK1 (p21 protein activated kinase 1) and MLK3 (mixed-lineage kinase 3) (Hodis et al., 2012; Krauthammer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The P29S mutation increases the affinity of Rac1 for PAK1 and MLK3.
source: The P29S mutation was identified as one of the major somatic mutations in melanoma (Hodis et al., 2012; Krauthammer et al., 2012), and was shown to increase the affinity of Rac1 for the effectors PAK1 (p21 protein activated kinase 1) and MLK3 (mixed-lineage kinase 3) (Hodis et al., 2012; Krauthammer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The P29S mutation increases the affinity of Rac1 for the WRC.
source: Similarly, we found that the P29S mutation also increases the affinity of Rac1 for the WRC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down and actin assembly assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The final density map from cryo-EM has a resolution of 7.0 Å.
source: Using FSC = 0.143 as a cut-off, the density map has a resolution of 7.0 Å.
evidence: This is shown in the FSC curve in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The mini-WRC crystal structure could be unambiguously docked into the EM density map.
source: The mini-WRC crystal structure (PDB 3P8C) could be unambiguously docked into the EM density map, with the majority of the secondary structural elements fitting into the density without need for adjustment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The EM map shows no density for the V and C helices of the VCA region of WAVE1.
source: The EM map shows no density for the V and C helices of the VCA region of WAVE1 (Figure 2B, right panel, elements colored black), which was present in the mini-WRC crystal structure but was removed in the ΔWRC230-Rac1 complex used here.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No density was observed for the first helix (α1) of Sra1.
source: No density was observed for the first helix (α1) of Sra1 (Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In crystals of mini-WRC, the first helix of Sra1 did not bind in intra-complex fashion, but rather to an adjacent WRC in the crystal lattice.
source: In crystals of mini-WRC this helix did not bind in intra-complex fashion, but rather to an adjacent WRC in the crystal lattice.
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: No major conformational changes of the WRC were observed within the limits of 7 Å resolution, except for the meander region of WAVE1.
source: No major conformational changes of the WRC were observed within the limits of our 7 Å resolution, except for the meander region of WAVE1 (a.a. 90–184) (Figure 2C), which formed a series of helices (α2-α6) arrayed across the surface of Sra1 in the mini-WRC crystal structure (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and compared to previous crystal structures.

claim: The meander region generally has weak density in the EM map.
source: In the EM map, the meander region generally has weak density.
evidence: This is observed in the EM density map.

claim: In the crystal structure of the inhibited mini-WRC, helices α2 and α6 directly bind the V and C regions of the VCA, respectively.
source: In the crystal structure of the inhibited mini-WRC, helices α2 and α6 directly bind the V and C regions of the VCA, respectively.
evidence: This is based on previously reported crystal structures.

claim: Mutagenesis studies suggest that interactions between helices α2 and α6 and the VCA act cooperatively to sequester the VCA, inhibiting its activity toward the Arp2/3 complex.
source: Mutagenesis studies suggest that these interactions act cooperatively to sequester the VCA, inhibiting its activity toward the Arp2/3 complex (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: Removing the VCA destabilizes the meander region.
source: The observations here support this idea, since removing the VCA (and possibly Rac1 binding as well) reciprocally appears to destabilize the meander region.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak density of the meander region in the EM map.

claim: The only major extra density not accounted for by the WRC was located on a surface of Sra1 ~120 Å from the previously proposed Rac1 binding site.
source: The only major extra density not accounted for by the WRC was located on a surface of Sra1 ~120 Å from the previously proposed Rac1 binding site, on the opposite end of the long axis of the WRC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the EM density map in Figure 1B.

claim: The extra density unambiguously accommodated the crystal structure of Rac1 P29S, including all secondary structure elements and most loops.
source: This density unambiguously accommodated the crystal structure of Rac1 P29S, including all secondary structure elements and most loops (PDB 3SBD) (Krauthammer et al., 2012) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The N terminus of Rac1 is located ~100 Å from the last ordered residue of WAVE1 to which it is linked.
source: In this position, the N terminus of Rac1 is located ~100 Å from the last ordered residue of WAVE1 to which it is linked, a distance that could readily be spanned by the 88 disordered residues of the tether.
evidence: This is measured from the EM structure.

claim: Small GTPases use two conserved structural elements, Switch I and Switch II, to bind and activate downstream signaling proteins in a nucleotide-dependent manner.
source: Rac1 and other small GTPases use two conserved structural elements, Switch I (a.a. 25–39) and Switch II (a.a. 57–75), to bind and activate downstream signaling proteins in a nucleotide-dependent manner (Mott and Owen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Both Switch I and Switch II of Rac1 make direct contact with the WRC through a conserved surface on the Sra1 subunit.
source: In our model of the complex, both Switch I and Switch II of Rac1 make direct contact with the WRC, through a conserved surface on the Sra1 subunit (a.a. 957–979, arrow heads in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the EM structure model in Figure 1C.

claim: The A Site is a conserved surface patch on Sra1 near the α4-α6 helices of the WAVE1 meander region, adjacent to the VCA binding site.
source: That site is a conserved surface patch on Sra1 near the α4-α6 helices of the WAVE1 meander region, adjacent to the VCA binding site (Figure 1B, Figure 3A) (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1B and 3A and referenced to previous work.

claim: In the EM reconstruction, Rac1 binds to a different conserved surface at the opposite end of the rod-shaped Sra1 subunit, which is distant from the meander-VCA region.
source: Instead, in the EM reconstruction, Rac1 binds to a different conserved surface at the opposite end of the rod-shaped Sra1 subunit, which is distant from the meander-VCA region (Figure 1B, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the EM structure in Figures 1B and 3A.

claim: Mutating any of three surface residues (C179R, R190D, or M632D) at the A Site disrupted Rac1 binding in qualitative GST pull-down experiments.
source: We showed that mutating any of three surface residues (C179R, R190D, or M632D), or one pair of residues (E434K/F626A), at the A Site disrupted Rac1 binding in qualitative GST pull-down experiments, and that the two mutations analyzed in a quantitative equilibrium dialysis experiment (R190D and E434K/F626A) both decreased affinity (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The D Site is conserved, although less so than the A Site.
source: In comparison, the D Site is also conserved, although less so than the A Site (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GST-Rac1 loaded with GMPPNP could efficiently retain wild type WRC as well as the D1122A/E1123A mutant.
source: GST-Rac1 loaded with GMPPNP (a poorly hydrolyzable GTP analog) could efficiently retain wild type (WT) WRC as well as one of the six D Site mutants, D1122A/E1123A (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the pull-down assay in Figure 3E.

claim: All D Site mutations except D1122A/E1123A substantially diminished binding to GST-Rac1.
source: All other mutations at the D Site substantially diminished binding, suggesting that this region mediates high-affinity interactions with Rac1.
evidence: This is shown in the pull-down assay in Figure 3E.

claim: The A Site mutation C179R decreased binding to GST-Rac1, albeit more moderately than most D Site mutations.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Chen et al., 2010), the A Site mutation, C179R, also decreased binding under the same experimental conditions, albeit more moderately (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the pull-down assay in Figure 3E.

claim: The observed interactions between Rac1 and the WRC are specific to active Rac1, since Rac1-GDP did not bind to any of the WRCs.
source: The observed interactions are specific to active Rac1, since Rac1-GDP did not bind to any of the WRCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the pull-down assay in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The S969F mutation did not appreciably affect binding to Rac1.
source: The S969F mutation did not appreciably affect binding (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in the pull-down assay in Figure 3E.

claim: P963 and Y967 are highly conserved in eukaryotic organisms including animals, fungi, amoebas and many protozoans, except plants.
source: It is notable that P963 and Y967 are highly conserved in eukaryotic organisms including animals, fungi, amoebas and many protozoans, except plants (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in the conservation analysis in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mutating either the A Site (C179R) or the D Site (Y967A) significantly decreased membrane recruitment of the WRC.
source: Paralleling the above GST pull-down experiments, mutating either the A Site (C179R) or the D Site (Y967A) significantly decreased membrane recruitment of the WRC, with the D Site mutation having a larger effect.
evidence: This is shown in the membrane recruitment assay in Figure 3F.

claim: The D Site mutation (Y967A) had a larger effect on membrane recruitment than the A Site mutation (C179R).
source: Paralleling the above GST pull-down experiments, mutating either the A Site (C179R) or the D Site (Y967A) significantly decreased membrane recruitment of the WRC, with the D Site mutation having a larger effect.
evidence: This is shown in the membrane recruitment assay in Figure 3F.

claim: The S969F mutation did not decrease, but rather slightly increased membrane recruitment.
source: In contrast, the S969F mutation did not decrease, but rather slightly increased membrane recruitment (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in the membrane recruitment assay in Figure 3F.

claim: Two molecules of Rac1 can simultaneously bind to a single WRC.
source: Increasing the concentration of EGFP-Rac1 up to 15.1 μM shifted the sedimentation coefficient of the WRC peak to 12.1S and stoichiometry to 1.9:1, confirming that two Rac1 molecules can simultaneously bind to a single WRC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the AUC data in Figure 4B.

claim: For the A Site mutant (C179R), at a nearly saturating concentration of EGFP-Rac1, the binding stoichiometry only reached 1:1.
source: For the A Site mutant (C179R), at a nearly saturating concentration of EGFP-Rac1 (8.4 μM vs. dissociation constant KD of 0.27 μM as determined below), the binding stoichiometry only reached 1:1 (Figure 4A, blue curves, 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the AUC data in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: For the D Site mutant (Y967A), the binding stoichiometry only reached 0.6:1 with 8.5 μM Rac1.
source: For the D Site mutant (Y967A), the binding stoichiometry only reached to 0.6:1 with 8.5 μM Rac1, consistent with the lower affinity (KD ~11.5 μM) of the A Site as determined below (Figure 4A, red curves, 4B) and implicated by the qualitative GST-pull down data above.
evidence: This is shown in the AUC data in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The AUC data confirmed that two molecules of Rac1 can engage the WRC at the A and D sites simultaneously.
source: Together, the AUC data confirmed that two molecules of Rac1 can engage the WRC at the A and D sites simultaneously, and that our mutations could selectively weaken binding to the individual sites.
evidence: This is shown in the AUC data in Figure 4.

claim: The dissociation constant for the D Site (KD,D) is 0.169 ± 0.008 μM.
source: Fitting to a simplified sequential two-site binding model or to a single-site model resulted in a similar dissociation constant for the D Site (KD,D of 0.169 ± 0.008 μM in Figure 5C, black solid curve compared to 0.106 ± 0.002 μM in Figure 5C, grey dotted curve).
evidence: This is derived from equilibrium pull-down assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The dissociation constant for the A Site when the D Site is bound (KD,A(D)) is 0.262 ± 0.044 μM.
source: Fitting to the sequential two-site binding model was statistically better than the single-site model (p=5.45×10−9), and yielded a dissociation constant for the A Site for the D Site-bound WRC (KD,A(D)) of 0.262 ± 0.044 μM, suggesting positive cooperativity between the A and D Sites compared to the dissociation constant for the A Site alone (KD,A of 11.52 ± 0.11 µM as determined below).
evidence: This is derived from equilibrium pull-down assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The dissociation constant for the A Site alone (KD,A) is 11.52 ± 0.11 μM.
source: Fitting to the sequential two-site binding model was statistically better than the single-site model (p=5.45×10−9), and yielded a dissociation constant for the A Site for the D Site-bound WRC (KD,A(D)) of 0.262 ± 0.044 μM, suggesting positive cooperativity between the A and D Sites compared to the dissociation constant for the A Site alone (KD,A of 11.52 ± 0.11 µM as determined below).
evidence: This is derived from equilibrium pull-down assays for the Y967A mutant shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is positive cooperativity between the A and D Sites.
source: Fitting to the sequential two-site binding model was statistically better than the single-site model (p=5.45×10−9), and yielded a dissociation constant for the A Site for the D Site-bound WRC (KD,A(D)) of 0.262 ± 0.044 μM, suggesting positive cooperativity between the A and D Sites compared to the dissociation constant for the A Site alone (KD,A of 11.52 ± 0.11 µM as determined below).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in KD values.

claim: The D Site has approximately 40-fold higher affinity for Rac1 than the A Site.
source: In summary, our data demonstrate that both the previously identified A Site and the newly identified D Site are bona fide binding sites for Rac1, the latter with ~40 fold higher affinity than the former.
evidence: This is calculated from the ratio of KD values (11.52/0.265 ≈ 43).

claim: The two sites can act together to recruit the WRC to membranes containing active Rac1.
source: The two sites can act together to recruit the WRC to membranes containing active Rac1.
evidence: This is supported by the membrane recruitment assay data.

claim: A saturating concentration of Rac1 (10 μM) could produce actin-assembly rates equivalent to that of the constitutively active WAVE1 VCA peptide for the WT WRC.
source: For the WT WRC, a saturating concentration of Rac1 (10 μM) could produce actin-assembly rates equivalent to that of the constitutively active WAVE1 VCA peptide (dashed cyan curve in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the actin assembly assay in Figure 6A.

claim: Mutating the D Site (Y967A) or the A Site (C179R) completely abrogated WRC activation.
source: Mutating the D Site (Y967A, Figure 6B,E) or the A Site (C179A, Figure 6D,E) completely abrogated activation, suggesting that activation of the WRC requires binding of Rac1 to both sites.
evidence: This is shown in the actin assembly assays in Figures 6B, 6D, and 6E.

claim: Activation of the WRC requires binding of Rac1 to both sites.
source: Mutating the D Site (Y967A, Figure 6B,E) or the A Site (C179A, Figure 6D,E) completely abrogated activation, suggesting that activation of the WRC requires binding of Rac1 to both sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the actin assembly assays showing that mutations at either site abolish activation.

claim: The S969F mutant WRC was more sensitive to Rac1 than the WT WRC.
source: Interestingly, the S969F mutant, which had slightly higher affinity for Rac1 (Figure 3F), was more sensitive to the GTPase than was WT WRC (Figure 6A,C,E).
evidence: This is shown in the actin assembly assays in Figures 6A, 6C, and 6E.

claim: The S969F mutant WRC was fully activated by only 3 μM Rac1, instead of 10 μM required for WT WRC.
source: For example, the S969F mutant WRC was fully activated by only 3 μM Rac1, instead of 10 μM (green dashed curve in Figure 6C vs. cyan dashed curve in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the actin assembly assays in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: Engagement of a single site (primarily the D Site) is not sufficient to drive WRC activation.
source: The lack of response to WRC-Rac1 concentrations up to 80 nM suggests suggests that engagement of a single site (primarily the D Site, due to its high affinity) is not sufficient to drive WRC activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of actin assembly data in Figure 6F.

claim: Plotting actin assembly rate versus the concentration of WRC-(Rac1)2 yields a linear relationship.
source: Further, plotting actin assembly rate versus the concentration of WRC-(Rac1)2 yields a linear relationship (red data in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 6F.

claim: The specific activity of WRC-(Rac1)2 is approximately 0.22 nM actin/s/nM WRC-(Rac1)2.
source: The slope of this line gives a specific activity of ~0.22 nM actin/s/nM WRC-(Rac1)2.
evidence: This is calculated from the linear fit in Figure 6F.

claim: Engagement of both the A and D sites is necessary for WRC activation.
source: Together, the qualitative and quantitative actin assembly data show that engagement of both the A and D sites is necessary for WRC activation.
evidence: This is supported by the actin assembly data in Figure 6.

claim: Rac1 activates the WRC through two binding sites that are distinct from the VCA-binding surface of Sra1.
source: First, Rac1 activates the WRC through two binding sites that are distinct from the VCA-binding surface of Sra1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: The A Site and the D Site likely cooperate to trigger conformational changes that release the VCA.
source: Our current data suggest that the A Site and the D Site likely cooperate to trigger conformational changes that release the VCA.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both sites for activation.

claim: The requirement for engagement of Rac1 at both sites to activate the WRC may explain why major conformational changes were not observed in the current structure.
source: In the latter scenario, the requirement for engagement of Rac1 at both sites to activate the WRC may explain why we did not observe major conformational changes on the WRC in our current structure, in which only the D Site is occupied.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural observations.

claim: S969 in Sra1 is buried immediately underneath the D Site.
source: We found that S969 in Sra1 is buried immediately underneath the D Site.
evidence: This is shown in the structure in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: S969F in Sra1 facilitates Rac1 binding and WRC activation.
source: Unlike the previous hypothesis that this mutation may act by destabilizing the WRC, our results show that S969F in Sra1 facilitates Rac1 binding and WRC activation.
evidence: This is shown in the membrane recruitment and actin assembly assays.

claim: S969 may be part of the pathway for conformational propagation from the D Site to the VCA-binding pocket upon Rac1 binding.
source: It is possible that S969 may be part of the pathway for the conformational propagation from the D Site to the VCA-binding pocket upon Rac1 binding.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the location and effects of the S969F mutation.

claim: Excessive activation of the WRC by Rac1 might be responsible for the observed changes in cocaine response and neuronal morphology in mice with the S968F mutation in Cyfip2.
source: Assuming the S968F mutation in Cyfip2 has a similar biochemical effect, our data suggest that excessive activation of the WRC by Rac1 might be responsible for the observed changes in cocaine response and neuronal morphology.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the biochemical effects of the S969F mutation in Sra1.

claim: The WRC has a basic face and an acidic face.
source: One face of the WRC is highly basic, and the opposite face is highly acidic (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When the WRC is bound to the negatively charged inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, its basic surface will lie against the membrane and its acidic surface will face the cytoplasm.
source: This charge distribution suggests that when the WRC is bound to the negatively charged inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, and/or specific phospholipids such as PIP3, its basic surface will lie against the membrane and its acidic surface will face the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the charge distribution of the WRC.

claim: In the proposed membrane orientation, both Rac1 binding sites can be positioned to enable a bound GTPase to bury its prenylated tail in the bilayer.
source: In this orientation, both Rac1 binding sites can be positioned to enable a bound GTPase to bury its prenylated tail in the bilayer, consistent with an activation model involving simultaneous engagement of both sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model shown in Figure 7.

claim: The proposed membrane orientation is compatible with VCA release to interact with the Arp2/3 complex in the cytoplasm.
source: This orientation is also compatible with other potential interactions. For example, VCA can be readily released from above the membrane to interact with the Arp2/3 complex further in the cytoplasm (Chazeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and supported by a citation.

claim: WIRS-containing transmembrane receptors could reach the WIRS-binding site on the acidic face of the WRC through less than 23 residues.
source: In addition, WIRS-containing transmembrane receptors could reach the WIRS-binding site on the acidic face of the WRC through < 23 residues (or ~80 Å in distance; Figure 7A) (Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model shown in Figure 7A and supported by a citation.

claim: With few exceptions, the WIRS elements in previously predicted WIRS-containing receptors in humans are generally located more than 25 residues from their transmembrane sequence.
source: Indeed, with few exceptions, the WIRS elements in previously predicted WIRS-containing receptors in humans are generally located > 25 residues from their transmembrane sequence (not shown) (Chen et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: WRC activation requires simultaneous engagement of two Rac1 molecules at two distinct binding sites with approximately 40-fold different affinity.
source: Our data suggest that WRC activation requires simultaneous engagement of two Rac1 molecules at two distinct binding sites with ~40 fold different affinity.
evidence: This is supported by the biochemical and structural data presented.

claim: When the density of Rac1 at membranes is low, Rac1 should interact with the WRC preferentially through the high-affinity D Site, which on its own is not sufficient to trigger activation but primes the complex.
source: When the density of Rac1 at membranes is low, Rac1 should interact with the WRC preferentially through the high-affinity site, which on its own is not sufficient to trigger activation but primes the complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the affinity differences and activation requirements.

claim: The WRC only becomes activated when Rac1 density is sufficient to enable binding to both sites.
source: The WRC only becomes activated when Rac1 density is sufficient to enable binding to both sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both sites for activation.

claim: Activation of the WRC at membranes is likely non-linear with respect to Rac1 density.
source: Consequently, activation of the WRC at membranes is likely non-linear with respect to Rac1 density (note that technical limitations in working with low Rac1 density on membranes prevented us from examining this experimentally).
evidence: This is inferred from the bivalent binding model.

claim: The non-linear activation behavior could be harnessed by cells to determine precisely where and when to turn on actin assembly.
source: This behavior could be harnessed by cells to determine precisely where and when to turn on actin assembly.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the proposed activation mechanism.

claim: Rac1 and the Arf GTPase can cooperatively recruit and activate the WRC at membranes.
source: Analogous ideas have been suggested previously, based on observations that Rac1 and the Arf GTPase can cooperatively recruit and activate the WRC at membranes (Koronakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is unlikely that either the A or D site is also the binding site for Arf GTPase.
source: Given the low sequence homology between Rac1 and Arf (22% and 38% identity in Switch I and Switch II, respectively), we feel it is unlikely that either the A or D site that we have characterized is also the binding site for Arf.
evidence: This is inferred from the low sequence homology between Rac1 and Arf.
